facts.text: An urban civilisation, the Harappan Civilisation, developed in the Indian subcontinent approximately 4,500 years ago, with wide roads, town planning, trade and writing.
facts.quote: An urban civilisation developed in the Indian subcontinent approximately 4,500 years ago. It is known as 'Harappan Civilisation.' This civilisation was so advanced that its cities were marked with clean and wide roads, meticulous town planning, flourishing trade and the use of writing.

facts.text: Because many of its sites were found in the Indus valley, it is also called the Indus Valley Civilisation; a civilisation is named after the site where it was first discovered.
facts.quote: Many sites associated with this civilisation have been discovered in the Indus valley, hence, it is also known as 'Indus Valley Civilisation.' A civilisation is named after the site, where it was first discovered.

facts.text: Excavations at Harappa first began in 1921; Harappa is on the banks of the River Ravi in Punjab.
facts.quote: Excavations at Harappa first began in 1921. Harappa is situated on the banks of the River Ravi in Punjab. Therefore, this civilisation known as the 'Harappan Civilisation.'

facts.text: The ancient river valley civilisations: Tigris-Euphrates (Mesopotamia), Nile (Egypt), Huang-Ho (China), Indus (Harappa).
facts.quote: The ancient river valley civilisations develope in vicinity of rivers. These were Tigris-Euphrates (Mesopotamia), Nile (Egypt), Huang-Ho (China), Indus (Harappa).

facts.text: Village settlements were set up where water, fertile land and transport were available, which were all found on river banks.
facts.quote: Village settlements were established where needs like availability of water, fertile land and system of transport were satisfied. All these factors were available on the river banks.

facts.text: The Early Harappan Period (approx. 3300 to 2600 BCE) saw a gradual transition from villages to cities, the beginning of urbanisation.
facts.quote: The initial phase of village settlements within the Harappan Civilisation is known as the Early Harappan Period (approx. 3300 to 2600 BCE). During this period, a gradual transition from villages to cities took place, marking the beginning of the process of 'urbanisation'.

facts.text: The Mature Harappan Period (approx. 2600 to 1900 BCE) was the most flourishing period; Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Dholavira and Lothal flourished then.
facts.quote: The Mature Harappan Period (approx. 2600 to 1900 BCE) is considered as the most flourishing period of the Harappan Civilisation. ... Major centers of the civilisatio such as Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Dholavira and Lothal flourished during this period.

facts.text: The Late Harappan Period (approx. 1900 to 1300 BCE) marks the gradual decline; major centres were destroyed or abandoned.
facts.quote: The Late Harappan Period (approx. 1900 to 1300 BCE) marks the phase when the Harappan Civilisation gradually began to decline. Its major centers were destroyed or abandoned.

facts.text: Many Harappan settlements were in the Indus basin, whose fertile soil boosted agriculture; settlements were along riverbanks.
facts.quote: A large number of settlements of the Harappan Civilisation were found in Indus basin. The fertile soil in this region provided a significant boost to agriculture. Thus, Harappan settlements were established along the riverbanks.

facts.text: Prominent Harappan sites: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Chanhudaro.
facts.quote: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Chanhudaro are some of the prominent Harappan sites.

facts.text: The Harappan Civilisation covered approximately 1.5 million square kilometers.
facts.quote: The geographical extent of this civilisation covered an area of approximately 1.5 million square kilometers.

facts.text: It extended from Manda in Jammu and Kashmir in the north, to Dholavira and Lothal in Gujarat, up to Daimabad in Ahilyanagar district; west to Balochistan (Pakistan), east to Alamgirpur in Uttar Pradesh.
facts.quote: The Harappan Civilisation extended from Manda in Jammu and Kashmir in the north, to Dholavira and Lothal in Gujarat and further upto Daimabad in Ahilyanagar district of Maharashtra. The Harappan Civilisation reached as far as Balochistan (in present-day Pakistan) to the west, while to the east, its extent reached Alamgirpur in Uttar Pradesh.

facts.text: Trade with distant regions was a primary factor in the wide expansion of the Harappan Civilisation.
facts.quote: Trade with distant regions was a primary factor contributing to the widespread expansion of the Harappan Civilisation.

facts.text: Distinctive Harappan features: town planning, well planned roads, well-built houses, excellent drainage, seals with inscriptions, high-quality pottery and toys.
facts.quote: Town planning, well planned roads, well-built houses, excellent drainage system, seals bearing inscriptions, high-quality pottery and various types of toys are the distinctive features of the Harappan Civilisation.

facts.text: Harappan houses were mainly built using baked bricks.
facts.quote: The houses of Harappan people were mainly built by using baked bricks.

facts.text: English Bond masonry: two headers and two stretchers used alternately; bricks in ratio 1:2:4; it kept homes safe from floods, earthquakes and wear and tear.
facts.quote: The method employed by the people of the Harappan Civilisation for constructing houses is generally known as the 'English Bond' masonry. In this method, while building a wall, two headers and two stretchers were used alternatively. ... A typical brick used to have a ratio of 1:2:4. Harappan people adopted this method to ensure the safety of their homes from floods, earthquakes and the gradual wear and tear

facts.text: Harappan houses had a central courtyard surrounded by rooms, with a well and a toilet near the entrance.
facts.quote: The houses featured a central courtyard surrounded by rooms, along with a well and a toilet situated near the entrance.

facts.text: Baked earthen conduits drained waste water; street drains were made of bricks and kept properly covered, showing awareness of public health.
facts.quote: Baked earthen conduits were utilized to drain waste water out of every house. Noteworthy feature was that the street drains were constructed using bricks and were kept properly covered. This demonstrates their high degree of awareness they possessed regarding public health.

facts.text: Harappan streets were broad and in a grid pattern; cities had two or more sections, each with its own fortification wall.
facts.quote: The streets in Harappan cities were broad and laid out in a grid pattern. Houses were built in the rectangular blocks created by them. The cities were generally divided into two or more sections. Each section had a separate fortification wall.

facts.text: The north-west section on elevated ground was the Citadel, likely home of administrators; the section south of it was for common residents.
facts.quote: The section at north-west was constructed on elevated ground, which is called as 'Citadel'. It is likely that administrators resided in Citadel. The section at the south of Citadel was occupied by common residents.

facts.text: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro: a tank about 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.5 m deep, of baked bricks, surrounded by small rooms; perhaps used for religious rituals.
facts.quote: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro is an unique example of the Harappan architecture. Some scholars are of the opinion that some religious rituals were performed within the Great Bath complex ... a large water tank measuring approximately 12 meters in length, 7 meters in width and 2.5 meters in depth. It was constructed using baked bricks. ... The tank was surrounded by a series of small rooms.

facts.text: Staple Harappan diet: wheat, barley, peas, sesame seeds, finger millet (Ragi), lentils and pulses; milk, meat and fish in some regions.
facts.quote: Wheat, barley, peas, sesame seeds, finger millet (Ragi), lentils and various types of pulses formed staple diet of the people. Archaeological evidence suggests that milk, meat and fish were also consumed in certain regions.

facts.text: Harappan pottery motifs were painted black on red, such as fish scales, intersecting circles and Pipal leaves.
facts.quote: These motifs were painted in black on a red-colored background. The decorative motifs include symbols such as fish scales, intersecting circles, Pipal leaves etc.

facts.text: Harappan people used cotton and silk garments; men and women wore a knee-length skirt and an upper garment.
facts.quote: Harappan, people used cotton and silk garments. ... Both men and women used a knee-length skirt and an upper garment.

facts.text: Harappan beads of clay, semi-precious stones, shells, copper, silver and gold were in high demand especially in Mesopotamia.
facts.quote: They made beads using clay, colourful semi-precious stones, shells, copper, silver and gold. These beads were in high demand especially in Mesopotamia.

facts.text: Wheat and barley were the principal Harappan crops; they were familiar with cotton.
facts.quote: Wheat and barley were their principal crops. The people of the Harappan Civilisation were familiar with cotton.

facts.text: Harappans were familiar with sailing, which enabled long-distance trade.
facts.quote: They were familiar with sailing, which enabled them to conduct long-distance trade.

facts.text: The world's oldest ploughed field was found at Kalibangan, on the Ghaggar River in Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan; they grew wheat, barley and chickpeas.
facts.quote: The world's oldest ploughed agricultural field has been discovered at Kalibangan. This site is situated on the banks of the Ghaggar River, in the Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan. ... They cultivated a variety of grains, including wheat, barley, and chickpeas.

facts.text: Kalibangan also has fire altars, perhaps for religious rituals, a planned drainage system, brick houses and seals.
facts.quote: Another distinctive feature of Kalibangan is the discovery of fire altars, which were perhaps used for performing religious rituals. ... this site also features a planned drainage system, brick-built houses and samples of seals.

facts.text: Harappans traded with Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) and Egypt in beads, jewellery, pottery and cotton, and imported metals and precious stones.
facts.quote: They were engaged in the exchange of goods with regions corresponding to Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) and Egypt. They traded in beads, jewellery, pottery and cotton. In exchange, they imported metals, precious stones and other commodities.

facts.text: Faience is a glass-like material in shades of blue, green and turquoise; faience goods from Harappa reached Sumer in southern Mesopotamia.
facts.quote: Faience is a glass-like material, having in shades of blue, green and turquoise. Faience bangles, beads and jewellery produced in Harappa reached Sumer in southern Mesopotamia in large quantities via established trade routes.

facts.text: Carnelian, a reddish-hued gemstone, was made into long and spherical beads traded in Mesopotamia.
facts.quote: Carnelian, a reddish-hued gemstone, was fashioned into both long and spherical beads. These beads were traded in Mesopotamia, where they were used in jewellery as well as making religious artifacts.

facts.text: Goddess Inanna, a prominent Sumerian deity, used Lapis Lazuli as a symbol of her divine grandeur.
facts.quote: Goddess Inanna was a prominent deity in Sumerian culture. ... Goddess Inanna used Lapis Lazuli as a symbol of her divine grandeur.

facts.text: Lapis Lazuli is a deep-blue semiprecious stone; its mines are in Afghanistan; it was in high demand in Mesopotamia.
facts.quote: Lapis Lazuli is a deep-blue semiprecious stone. ... Mines of Lapis Lazuli are located in Afghanistan. Harappan merchants were actively engaged in the trade of this stone, It was in high demand in Mesopotamia.

facts.text: Lothal was a significant Harappan port with a massive dockyard; trade went along the Arabian Sea coast as far as the Persian Gulf.
facts.quote: During Harappan period Lothal served as a significant port. A massive dockyard has been discovered at this site. The trade of the Harappan civilisation extended along the coast of the Arabian Sea, reaching as far as the Persian Gulf.

facts.text: Harappan seals were used primarily for trade; they show ox, elephant, buffalo, rhinoceros, tiger and human figures.
facts.quote: The Harappan seals were used primarily for trade purposes. These seals have animal pictures such as ox, elephant, buffalo, rhinoceros and tiger as well as human figures.

facts.text: A bronze figurine from the Harappan civilisation is famously known as the Dancing Girl.
facts.quote: A bronze figurine discovered from the Harappan civilisation is famously known as the 'Dancing Girl'.

facts.text: A distinctive statue unearthed at Mohenjodaro, now in the National Museum, Delhi, is identified as the Priest-King.
facts.quote: An important artifact of the Harappan civilisation is a distinctive statue discovered at Mohenjodaro. This statue was unearthed during excavations at Mohenjodaro and is currently housed in the National Museum, Delhi. It is identified as the 'Priest-King'.

facts.text: Harappan clay toys include bulls, dogs, elephants, wheeled carts, spinning tops and whistles.
facts.quote: These toys were made of clay. They include animal figurines such as bulls, dogs and elephants as well as wheeled carts, spinning tops and whistles.

facts.text: A shift in a river's course may have caused water scarcity; natural calamities like floods, droughts or earthquakes may also have caused the decline.
facts.quote: Perhaps a shift in the river's course led to water scarcity, which, in turn, adversely affected agriculture and daily life. Another reason might be natural calamities such as massive floods, droughts, or earthquakes.

facts.text: Around 2300 BCE, trade with the Sumerian civilisation began to slow down, beginning the Harappan decline.
facts.quote: Around 2300 BCE, trade with the Sumerian civilisation began to slow down, causing the beginning of the decline of Harappan civilisation.

facts.text: Sargon, a powerful king of the Akkadian Empire, saw maritime trade flourish between Mesopotamia and the Harappan civilisation in Lapis Lazuli, gold, silver, copper and beads.
facts.quote: Sargon was a powerful king of the Akkadian Empire. Evidence suggests that, during his reign maritime trade flourished between Mesopotamia and the Harappan civilisation. This trade involved the exchange of valuable commodities such as Lapis Lazuli, gold, silver, copper, beads and other precious items.

facts.text: After Sargon's era, political instability in Mesopotamia halted the trade; the Harappan economy was endangered and people migrated from cities to smaller villages.
facts.quote: following the era of Sargon, political instability emerged in Mesopotamia. ... the trade that had flourished during Sargon's time gradually came to a halt. As a result, the economy of the Harappan cities was endangered. Trade declined and people began migrating from the cities toward smaller villages.

facts.text: The influence of the Harappan Civilisation was not diminished; it forms the base of our cultural legacy.
facts.quote: However the influence of the Harappan Civilisation was not diminished. ... Thus, the Harappan Civilisation was a prosporous one and it forms the base of our cultural legacy.
